Local-problem teaching connects practice, source, affected people, and evidence. Climate teaching traces harm to farms, incomes, homes, and schools. The framework section explains how assessments, training, participation, and monitoring guide local plans.

The lesson limits single-event climate attribution, rejects blame without evidence, distinguishes temporary weather from trends, allows overlapping social/economic effects and dual-purpose projects, and requires checking actual results instead of a program name.

general-information-environment-manageme.quote: Look for the harmful practice, its likely source, and who or what is affected.
general-information-environment-manageme.note: Teaches systematic problem identification and separates causes from effects.

general-information-environment-manageme.quote: For suspected water pollution, officials can inspect possible sources and test water samples.
general-information-environment-manageme.note: Explains inspection and testing mechanisms and the DENR/EMB role.

general-information-environment-manageme.quote: It can also reduce water supplies or damage coasts and farms.
general-information-environment-manageme.note: Adds local climate effects and distinguishes climate from a single weather event.

general-information-environment-manageme.quote: Governments choose climate laws, budgets, land-use rules, and projects.
general-information-environment-manageme.note: Explains policy choices and works a budgeting and coordination case.

general-information-environment-manageme.quote: Flooding can force families to move and keep children out of school.
general-information-environment-manageme.note: Explains effects on homes and schooling and applies them in Example 5.

general-information-environment-manageme.note: Explains framework content and applies assessment, training, inclusion, and review in Example 8.
